newsitem.title: UK: LME--Enhancements on course a year after Sumitomo.
newsitem.headline: LME--Enhancements on course a year after Sumitomo.

text.p: One year after the multi-billion Sumitomo Corp scandal erupted, the London Metal Exchange (LME) is well into the process of instituting reforms.
"To date, we are about half-way through this implementation process," LME Chief Executive David King said.

In June 1996, Japan's Sumitomo stunned the metals world by announcing losses that were eventually put at $2.6 billion, sustained during 10 years of unauthorised copper trading carried out by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.
"These events were the failure of a firm to properly control the activities of an employee," King said in an interview.

He said that the LME's action in investigating its copper market, which started in autumn 1995, alongside separate probes by the U.K. and U.S. regulatory authorities, were instrumental in Sumitomo uncovering Hamanaka's activites.

The LME, which was nevertheless criticised by some quarters, called in Britain's top markets regulator, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB), to carry out a wide-ranging review of the Exchange in the days that followed Sumitomo's bombshell.
The SIB delivered its report in December 1996, calling for a package of wide-ranging enhancements.
"It is important to note that users are happy with the way the LME operates and seek no changes, and SIB identified no systemic risks," King said.
Since January, the LME has addressed governance, increasing the size of its board from 16 to 18 directors.
"This enhanced the capacity to have independent and non-conflicted directors on the Board," King said.
This goes some way to tackling the vexed issue of "conflicts of interest" when the board is called upon to intervene in the market.
King said that these steps should be seen as evolutionary, rather then revolutionary.
"We can consider further revisions with the passing of time," he added.

As part of moving powers away from the board, the LME has increased the size of its various committees. In future, they will have more powers delegated to them. There are around 100 participants on LME committees.
"There are more producer and consumer representatives on the committees. It gives them more input into the operation of the exchange," King said.
And by devolving powers down from the Board, the committees have to accept more responsibility.
Changes in warehousing and inventory reporting continue apace as well, as this was an area where the the SIB review threw up many grumbles.
Many industry participants were concerned over differences regarding in-to-out charges, storage incentives, and the slowness of outgoing deliveries, King said.
"We propose to address these differences with the warehouse companies," he said.
The LME appears to have found a way via its contractual agreements with warehouse firms to do this, he added.
Meanwhile, this week the Board decided that daily stock reporting, introduced in April, would become permanent, as this has been well received.
Also, from October the Exchange will break down its warehouse stock figures to show metal that has been taken off-warrant, but not shipped out, as separate data.
Despite other changes and refinements that may yet come, including an automated warrant transfer system, the industry should not get pre-occupied with the issue of stock transparency.
"People should not get mesmerised - it can never be a total picture as LME warehouses have less than 50 percent of total stocks," King said.

By the end of the year the vast majority of the SIB recommendations should be in place. Where there would be an overrun, it would be because the LME has yet to decide whether to go ahead on, say, an automated warrant transfer system.
"The market came through Sumitomo...once the SIB recommendations have been implemented the Exchange will be a stronger, more attractive place to do business," King said.
